newsitem.title: UK: Agony and ecstasy etched on election faces.
newsitem.headline: Agony and ecstasy etched on election faces.

text.p: Raw emotion was written on the faces of victor and vanquished when Britain's Labour Party swept to the biggest election victory in its history on Friday.
Labour leader Tony Blair choked back tears. Conservatives talked of a dark and terrible night for a party hit by a "tidal wave" of rejection.

Blair's composure cracked as he remembered his late mother. "All that could have made this moment complete was that my mother was here as well," he told cheering supporters as he acknowledged his party was heading for government.
His deputy, John Prescott, could barely disguise his delight, grinning from ear to ear as Labour swept to a landslide victory.

New Labour lawmaker Ben Bradshaw, who openly admitted he was gay, celebrated his victory over Conservative morals campaigner Adrian Rogers by thanking voters for "rejecting bigotry and choosing tolerance".

But the Conservatives looked like shell-shocked victims in the electoral trenches. Bitterness and recrimination rose rapidly to the surface. The agony of defeat was etched on the faces of scores of defeated candidates.
"It has been a dark night for Conservatives," interior minister Michael Howard said after winning his own seat but watching six of his cabinet colleagues losing theirs.

Prime Minister John Major, his hopes in ruins, said: "We have had great victories in our time, we have had defeats in our time. We accept them both, I hope, with a certain dignity and a certain grace."
Defeated Conservative David Mellor, who looked stunned by his defeat, summed up their astonishment: "A tidal wave has burst over the Conservative Party tonight."
He then lashed out angrily at Anglo-French billionaire Sir James Goldsmith, whose Referendum Party failed to secure a vote on Britain's continued membership of the European Union.
Goldsmith goaded Mellor, shouting "Out! Out! Out!" as the former minister gave a speech acknowledging defeat.
The composure of Defence Minister Michael Portillo cracked after he was defeated and lost his chance to challenge for leadership of the Conservtaive Party.
When pressed by a BBC interviewer Jeremy Paxman to come clean about the party's future, he said: "I am taking a night off. Oh Jeremy, do stop this nonsense."
But the most astonished man of the night was BBC war correspondent Martin Bell, more used to dodging bullets down Snipers Alley in Bosnia than fighting elections.

The reporter, sporting his trademark white suit, ran as an "anti-sleaze" candidate against former Conservative minister Neil Hamilton, who has denied allegations he took money from a businessman to ask questions in parliament.
When Bell announced his candidature as an independent he expected Hamilton to resign immediately. Bell would then have stepped down. Now Bell faces five years in parliament as an independent.
"I believe you have lit a beacon which will shed a light in some dark corners and illuminate the mother of parliaments itself. It is a message which will be heeded," he told supporters.
